strengths: The paper identifies a real bottleneck in reservoir computing: dense recurrent reservoirs are sequential and have quadratic parameter memory. The proposed diagonal complex recurrence with associative scan is a natural and useful way to make RC more accelerator-friendly.

The empirical results show clear efficiency advantages over traditional ESNs, especially on longer sequences and sMNIST/psMNIST, with lower training time, energy, and emissions while preserving competitive accuracy in several settings.

The paper is generally readable, with a clear architecture description, complexity discussion, and a broad set of RC-oriented benchmarks including memory, forecasting, UCR/UEA classification, and pixel-level MNIST tasks.

The appendix includes useful implementation details: dataset splits, hyperparameter search ranges, computational resources, model selection protocol, and additional comparisons to SCR and structured RC.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are overstated. Proposition 4.2 relies on exact diagonalization of an arbitrary transition matrix, but not every square matrix is diagonalizable; saying diagonalizable up to arbitrarily small perturbations does not prove exact functional equivalence. The ESP proof also does not handle the boundary case |lambda| = 1 in the necessity argument, despite the theorem requiring strict inequality.

The universality claim does not tightly match the actual model used in most experiments. The theory assumes a nonlinear MLP readout, whereas the main RC experiments use a fixed random mixing layer plus a linear ridge readout. This weakens the connection between the proof and the empirical ParalESN architecture.

The complexity analysis conflates parallel depth with total computational work. Associative scan gives O(log T) depth only under a strong processor assumption, while total work remains O(T); the paper’s O(log(T) Nh Nin) whole-sequence complexity and corresponding claims of logarithmic scaling are therefore potentially misleading as stated.

Originality is moderate. The core mechanism is very close to LRU/S5-style diagonal complex linear recurrences plus scan, applied in an untrained reservoir setting. The reservoir-computing framing is useful, but the method itself is mostly a recombination of known ingredients.

The empirical evidence supports efficiency more strongly than accuracy. On forecasting and memory tasks ParalESN is often comparable but not consistently better than deep ESN, and sometimes worse on MG84/NARMA10-like tasks. Strong claims such as being broadly more accurate than traditional RC are only partially supported.

The comparison to fully trainable sequence models is limited mainly to sMNIST/psMNIST, which are dated benchmarks and do not establish competitiveness with modern SSMs/Transformers on current long-sequence tasks. The forecasting experiments do not include the fully trainable baselines despite claiming integration with the deep learning landscape.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript cites external code for baselines but does not clearly state that the ParalESN implementation and scripts will be released. Search budgets are described, but the number of random seeds, Bayesian search details, and fairness of the 24-hour tuning budget across models are not sufficiently transparent.

Limitations are not discussed explicitly. Important caveats such as reliance on large parallel hardware, sensitivity to spectral/phase hyperparameters, theory-experiment mismatch, and the restricted benchmark scope should be acknowledged more directly.

strengths: The paper addresses a real bottleneck in reservoir computing: sequential recurrence and the memory cost of dense reservoirs. A diagonal complex recurrence with associative scan is a reasonable direction for improving parallelism and scalability.

The empirical scope is broader than many reservoir-computing papers, covering memory tasks, forecasting, UCR/UEA classification, and sequential MNIST variants, with comparisons to both ESN variants and trainable sequence models.

The paper includes some useful implementation details and appendices, including hyperparameter search ranges, dataset descriptions, computational resources, and an additional comparison to structured reservoir baselines.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are overstated and partly unsound. Proposition 4.2 claims exact equivalence between arbitrary linear ESNs and ParalESN via diagonalization, but not every square matrix is diagonalizable; the appendix only mentions diagonalizability up to perturbation, which does not imply exact equality of outputs. This undermines the stated equivalence and the subsequent universality framing.

The theory does not match the implemented model. The universality discussion relies on an arbitrary MLP readout, while the practical architecture uses a fixed random convolutional mixing layer plus a trained readout, and often only a linear/ridge readout. The paper does not prove that this random convolutional mixer/readout decomposition preserves the claimed expressivity.

The complexity claims are misleading. The paper states whole-sequence time complexity of O(log(T) Nh Nin), but associative scan reduces parallel depth only under a large-processor assumption; total work and memory over the sequence remain linear in T, and computing input projections across all time steps also costs linear work. Presenting this as a blanket reduction from linear to logarithmic time overstates the algorithmic improvement.

The experimental evidence does not convincingly support the strongest claims. ParalESN is often comparable rather than clearly better than deep ESN on regression tasks, and on several forecasting benchmarks it is worse than ESN/deep ESN. The strongest results are on classification and sMNIST/psMNIST, but these are relatively narrow and do not establish broad competitiveness with modern sequence models.

Efficiency comparisons are insufficiently controlled. Training-time, energy, and emissions measurements mix very different training procedures, model classes, hardware utilization patterns, and hyperparameter-search effects. The paper does not clearly separate recurrence runtime, readout fitting, model selection cost, GPU/CPU usage, or implementation maturity, making the practical speedup claims hard to interpret.

The baseline treatment is uneven. Comparisons to LSTM/Transformer/LRU/Mamba are only shown for MNIST-style tasks, not for the forecasting benchmarks where those models are highly relevant. Conversely, the reservoir baselines are mostly small fixed-size configurations, so it is unclear whether the gains come from the proposed recurrence, tuning differences, or architectural choices such as depth and mixing.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful appendices. The manuscript gives hyperparameter ranges and resources but does not provide enough detail on random seeds, number of trials, Bayesian search budget per model/task, exact implementations of associative scan and complex operations, or whether timing includes validation/model selection. Code availability is not clearly stated.

Presentation has several clarity and rigor issues, including ambiguous notation, grammatical errors, inconsistent claims about trainable versus untrained components, and figures based on normalized aggregate scores that obscure absolute task-level behavior. The paper also lacks a serious limitations discussion, especially around processor assumptions, memory scaling with stored states, applicability beyond fixed-length offline processing, and the gap between theory and the actual random-feature implementation.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful modernization of reservoir computing: replacing dense sequential reservoir dynamics with complex diagonal linear recurrence plus a fixed nonlinear mixing layer, enabling parallel scan over time and much lower parameter memory than dense ESNs.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the reservoir-computing setting, covering memory tasks, synthetic and real forecasting, UCR/UEA classification, and sequential/permuted MNIST. The results consistently show large speed and energy gains over traditional ESNs, with competitive or better accuracy in many cases.
The comparison to shallow and deep ESNs is well targeted, and the structured-RC appendix comparison helps show that the gains are not merely due to using any structured reservoir.
The paper is generally well written and easy to follow. The architecture, initialization, computational motivation, and experimental setup are described with enough detail to understand the method.

The work is significant for practitioners interested in reservoir computing because it addresses two practical bottlenecks: sequential recurrence and dense reservoir memory. The ability to scale reservoirs to much larger hidden sizes is a meaningful contribution.
weaknesses: The theoretical expressivity claim is somewhat overstated. Proposition 4.2 relies on diagonalizing an arbitrary transition matrix, but not every square matrix is diagonalizable; the appendix notes diagonalizability only up to arbitrarily small perturbations, which does not prove exact equivalence for every linear ESN as stated.

The universality discussion is less strong than it first appears because the formal analysis is for a simplified one-layer linear recurrence with a nonlinear readout, while the practical model uses fixed convolutional mixing and often only trains the final readout. The connection between the theorem and the actually evaluated architecture should be tightened.

The efficiency claims depend on idealized parallel scan complexity, including assumptions about available parallel processors. The paper reports strong wall-clock gains, but the asymptotic statement that sequence-length dependence becomes logarithmic should be presented more carefully in relation to hardware, memory traffic, and practical scan implementations.

The comparison to fully trainable modern sequence models is limited mostly to sMNIST/psMNIST, which are useful but dated benchmarks. The paper would be stronger with broader comparisons on current long-sequence or time-series benchmarks against SSM-style models, especially since the framing invokes SSMs and deep learning scalability.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives datasets, search spaces, hardware, and some external code sources, but I do not see a clear release of the authors' implementation or exact selected hyperparameters/seeds for each benchmark. The 24-hour Bayesian search also complicates reproducing the reported efficiency results if search cost is excluded from training time.

Some experimental choices need clearer fairness justification, especially the different readout choices across tasks, parameter matching between trainable and reservoir models, and whether model selection budgets were equalized across all baselines.
